title: Man. Post. Cap. I: Confession XI vitium; Garissoles Cap. V–IX infant-death imputation
pass_a_gloss: You indeed, observant fellow-initiate, believe the foregoing. But of this last what do you feel? It is framed in the words of the confession of our Churches, Article XI, which you yourself praise in Cap. VII: We believe this vice to be truly sin, which makes all and singular men, not even little ones excepted still hiding in the womb of mothers, guilty of eternal death before God. We also affirm that this vice, even after baptism, is truly sin as far as guilt is concerned. This I believe from the heart as agreeing with the sacred letters, nay with reason, and it cannot be overturned without the very compacting and context of my theses which you attack being disordered. But do you believe it? You seem to affirm such a thing in Cap. I and II of your tractate and in some other places: but I fear you so speak for the sake of hiding your opinion: for in certain other places you expressly deny it, and on that negation as a foundation a not contemptible part of this your disputation rests. Recognize your words: for I will not mind transferring them hither. Cap. V you gather thus: Where death reigns, and there is no guilt from one's own actual sin, there necessarily is imputation of the guilt of the first sin. Likewise Cap. V: death reigned unto infants. Therefore the guilt of the first sin was necessarily imputed to infants. But when you saw it could be answered to you that the guilt in them is from inherent vice and hereditary depravation, you called this reply a cavil, and against it concluded thus: if children in the mothers' womb, or newly born, are sinners, they are so either because they have sinned in act, or because the first sin of the first parent is imputed to them. For a third cannot be given that constitutes them sinners. For one is called a sinner on account of sin; nor can any other sin be imputed except that first. Reread, if you please, what follows. Cap. IX you open your mind more fully. I do not see, you say, what original sin is if such imputation is denied. Could Pighius have expressed his opinion more clearly?
pass_b_english: You, observant colleague, hold the points above. But what of this last? It is cast in the words of our Churches' Confession, Article XI, which you yourself praise in chapter VII: We believe this vice is truly sin, which makes every person—even little ones still hidden in the womb—guilty of eternal death before God. We also affirm that after baptism this vice is still truly sin as to guilt. I believe this from the heart as agreeing with Scripture and with reason; overturn it and the very fabric of the theses you attack comes apart. Do you believe it? In chapters I-II of your tract and elsewhere you seem to say so; yet I fear you speak so to hide your view, for in other places you openly deny it, and a large part of your case rests on that denial. Hear your own words. Chapter V: Where death reigns and there is no guilt from one's own actual sin, there must be imputation of the first sin's guilt. Likewise: death reigned over infants; therefore the first sin's guilt was necessarily imputed to them. When you saw the reply that their guilt comes from inherent vice and hereditary depravity, you called it a cavil and concluded: if children in the womb or newly born are sinners, it is either because they have sinned in act or because the first parent's first sin is imputed to them—for no third way can make them sinners. One is called a sinner because of sin; no other sin can be imputed but that first. Read on. In chapter IX you speak more plainly: I do not see what original sin is if such imputation is denied. Could Pighius have put his mind more clearly?
source_text: Tu quidem, observande Symmysta, superiora credis. Sed de hoc ultimo quid sentis? Conceptum est verbis confessionis Ecclesiarum nostrarum Art. XI. quae tu ipse laudas Cap. VII. Credimus hoc vitium esse vere peccatum, quod omnes et singulos homines, ne parvulis quidem exceptis adhuc in utero matrum delitescentibus, aeternae mortis reos coram Deo peragit. Affirmamus quoque hoc vitium, etiam post baptismum, esse vere peccatum, quod ad culpam attinet. Hoc ego ex animo credo ut sacris literis consentaneum, immo rationi, neque everti potest, quin eo ipso thesium mearum quas oppugnas compactio et contextus luxetur. Tu vero num id credis? videris tale quid affirmare Cap. I. et II. tui tractatus, et aliis aliquot locis: sed vereor ne ita loquaris occultandae opinionis tuae gratia: Id enim aliis quibusdam locis exerte negas, eaque negatione tanquam fundamento pars non contemnenda hujus tuae disputationis nititur. Recognosce tua verba: non enim gravabor huc transferre. Cap. V. sic colligis, Ubi mors regnat, nec est reatus ex peccato proprio actuali, ibi necessario est imputatio reatus primi peccati. Item, Cap. V. mors regnavit in infantes. Ergo infantibus reatus primi peccati necessario fuit imputatus. Cum autem videres tibi responderi posse, reatum in illis esse a vitio inhaerente et depravatione haereditaria, tu hanc responsionem cavillum appellasti, et contra sic conclusisti, si pueri in utero matrum, aut recens nati, sunt peccatores, ideo sunt, vel quod actu peccaverint, vel quod primum peccatum primi parentis ipsis imputetur. Tertium siquidem dari non potest, quod illos constituat peccatores. Nam peccator quis dicitur ob peccatum; Nec ullum aliud peccatum potest imputari, nisi illud primum. Relege, si placet, quae sequuntur. Cap. IX. mentem tuam plenius aperis. Non video, inquis, quid sit peccatum originis si negetur ejusmodi imputatio. Potuisset-ne Pighius suam sententiam exprimere clarius?
